title: Al-'Asr: by time
hookLine: by time, people are in loss, except those who believe, do good, and urge truth and patience (Surah 103)

cards: Open the screen-time report on your phone. Most people do it once, wince, and never do it again. Four hours a day.

Twenty-eight hours a week. Numbers you'd never agree to if someone asked you to spend them up front. Time goes the way ice melts: not all at once, just steadily, while you're looking at something else.
Today's surah is one of the shortest in the Qur'an, three lines, and it opens by swearing an oath by that very thing.

teach.h: AL-'ASR — THE DECLINING DAY, AND TIME.
teach.b: Here's the whole surah in Pickthall's translation: By the declining day, Lo! man is in a state of loss, Save those who believe and do good works, and exhort one another to truth and exhort one another to endurance.
The first word, al-'asr, has several meanings, and scholars keep them all. It's the late afternoon, the declining day, when the light starts to go. It's the name of the afternoon prayer, 'asr.
And it's time itself, the age, an era. The root carries a sense of pressing, of squeezing something out: the afternoon is when you feel the day being squeezed.
When the Qur'an swears by something, it's asking you to look at it closely. So look at time.
Then the verdict: the human being is in loss. Not some people. All of us, by default.
Time runs out every hour, like capital being spent; that's the plain math of being mortal.
And then the exception, which is the rest of the surah: those who believe, who do good, who urge one another to truth, and to patience. Tomorrow, those four up close.

teach.h: EXCEPT: THE WAY OUT OF LOSS.
teach.b: Today, the oath and the loss. The surah doesn't tell you to panic. It tells you to notice.
Every hour is being spent on something.
By time is a question: on what?

how: Al-'Asr is among the most memorized surahs and is often recited in the prayers; its name is shared with the afternoon prayer, and many Muslims recall it when they think about how they spend their time.

o: time, and the late afternoon as day declines
the dawn prayer, said before sunrise
the night, when the day's work is done

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.

s: al-'Asr is one of the shortest surahs
the surah says only bad people are in loss
it says the human being is in loss, then names the exception.
it's the declining day, the afternoon prayer, and time itself.

games.q: the surah swears by time and says the human is in loss. what comes next?
o: an exception: those who believe, do good, and urge truth and patience
a description of the end of the world
games.why: the loss is the default, and the surah names the way out in the very next breath (103:3).

practice: Look at the clock and notice the time. Sit, and let the seconds go by without filling them; feel them pass, because they're passing either way.
Then choose, on purpose, one thing for your next five minutes instead of scrolling by default: a call to your mother, a page of something good, a walk around the block, tidying one shelf.

wordCard.voice: Al-'Asr. Time, the declining day, and the afternoon prayer; the name of Surah one hundred three. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: time, the late afternoon; also the afternoon prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: by time. Every afternoon, the light going down says it again. See you tomorrow.
